group.title: Health and medicine
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To find out what illness a person has by examining them.
examples: The doctor {diagnosed} a broken wrist after the X-ray.
wrong: The doctor diagnosed my illness without examining me or asking a single question.

words.meaning: To say officially which medicine a patient should take.
examples: The doctor {prescribed} antibiotics for my chest infection.
wrong: The doctor prescribed a new car for my headache.

words.meaning: A doctor who performs operations.
examples: The {surgeon} removed the patient’s appendix.
wrong: The surgeon cuts people’s hair at the shop on the corner.

words.meaning: Able to pass from one person to another, usually through the air or water.
examples: Flu is highly {infectious}, so stay at home.
wrong: The illness is infectious, so you can’t catch it from anyone.

words.meaning: Becoming ill when you touch, eat or breathe in a particular thing.
examples: I’m {allergic} to cats, so I start sneezing near them.
wrong: She’s allergic to peanuts, so she eats them every day without any problem.

words.meaning: A medicine that makes pain less strong.
examples: She took a {painkiller} for her headache.
wrong: He took a painkiller to make his headache worse.

words.meaning: Putting medicine into the body with a needle.
examples: The nurse gave him an {injection} in his arm.
wrong: The injection was a pill that she swallowed with water.

words.meaning: A large room in a hospital where patients stay.
examples: My grandmother is in the women’s {ward} on the fourth floor.
wrong: The ward is the car that takes patients to the hospital.

words.meaning: A crack or break in a bone.
examples: The X-ray showed a small {fracture} in his ankle.
wrong: The fracture showed that his bones were perfectly whole.

words.meaning: Bigger than usual because of an injury or illness.
examples: Her ankle was badly {swollen} after the fall.
wrong: After the bee sting, his hand was swollen and smaller than normal.

words.meaning: The feeling that you are going to be sick and bring food up.
examples: The boat trip gave me terrible {nausea}.
wrong: Her nausea made her want a huge meal right away.

words.meaning: A sudden serious illness when the heart stops working properly.
examples: He had a {heart attack} while shoveling snow.
wrong: A heart attack is a feeling of being in love.

words.meaning: A piece of thread used by a doctor to close a cut.
examples: The cut on her head needed six {stitches}.
wrong: The nurse put stitches in the wound to keep it open.

words.meaning: A condition in which you cannot sleep well.
examples: Stress at work gave her {insomnia} for months.
wrong: His insomnia made him sleep for twelve hours every night.

words.meaning: The state of being so overweight that it is dangerous to health.
examples: Poor diet and little exercise can lead to {obesity}.
wrong: Obesity is caused by being much too thin.

words.meaning: The number of years a person is likely to live.
examples: {Life expectancy} has risen thanks to better medicine.
wrong: Life expectancy is the number of years a person has already worked.

words.meaning: To start to have a minor illness.
examples: I think I’m {coming down with} a cold.
wrong: She came down with the flu, so she felt healthier than ever.

words.meaning: To suddenly become unconscious for a short time.
examples: It was so hot in the hall that two people {passed out}.
wrong: He passed out and stayed wide awake through the whole concert.

words.meaning: A doctor who knows a lot about one area of medicine.
examples: My doctor sent me to a skin {specialist}.
wrong: A specialist is a doctor who knows a little about everything but nothing in depth.

words.meaning: A large number of cases of a disease in one area at the same time.
examples: The town faced a flu {epidemic} last winter.
wrong: During the epidemic, only one person in the country got sick.

words.meaning: A person trained to prepare and sell medicines.
examples: Ask the {pharmacist} how often to take the tablets.
wrong: The pharmacist operates on patients in the hospital.

words.meaning: Containing germs that cause disease.
examples: Clean the cut so it doesn’t get {infected}.
wrong: The wound is infected, so it is perfectly clean and healthy.

words.meaning: A pain in your throat, often when you have a cold.
examples: I’ve got a {sore throat}, so it hurts to swallow.
wrong: My sore throat made it easier to swallow and sing.

words.meaning: A very bad headache that can also make you feel sick.
examples: Bright lights can give her a {migraine}.
wrong: A migraine is a mild pain in your little toe.

words.meaning: An illness that makes it hard to breathe at times.
examples: He carries an inhaler because he has {asthma}.
wrong: Her asthma helps her breathe more easily than anyone else.

words.meaning: An operation to put an organ from one person into another person’s body.
examples: She needs a kidney {transplant}.
wrong: A transplant is a pill you take for a cold.

words.meaning: Becoming ill again after seeming to get better.
examples: After a few good weeks, he suffered a {relapse}.
wrong: His relapse meant he was completely healthy again.

words.meaning: Something that cures an illness or makes it less painful.
examples: Honey and lemon is a good {remedy} for a cough.
wrong: The remedy made her cold much worse.

words.meaning: To lose blood from the body.
examples: His knee was {bleeding} after he fell off his bike.
wrong: The cut was bleeding, but there was no blood at all.

words.meaning: A person trained to give emergency medical help, often in an ambulance.
examples: The {paramedics} arrived within minutes of the crash.
wrong: The paramedic sells tickets at the train station.

words.meaning: A hospital department for people who are extremely ill and need constant care.
examples: After the accident, he spent a week in {intensive care}.
wrong: Patients go to intensive care when they only have a small cold.

words.meaning: The part of a hospital where people who need urgent help are treated.
examples: We rushed him to the {emergency room} after he cut his hand.
wrong: You go to the emergency room for a routine eye test next month.

words.meaning: To officially let a patient leave the hospital.
examples: She was {discharged} from the hospital after three days.
wrong: The hospital discharged him, so he had to stay in his bed there.

words.meaning: Medicine that a doctor gives you for an illness.
examples: Take your {medication} twice a day with food.
wrong: Medication is the food you eat at the hospital.

words.meaning: The sudden start of a disease that affects many people.
examples: There was an {outbreak} of food poisoning at the school.
wrong: The outbreak meant that no one in the city was ill.

words.meaning: A period when a person or animal is kept apart so a disease doesn’t spread.
examples: The travelers were kept in {quarantine} for ten days.
wrong: During quarantine, he visited hundreds of people.

words.meaning: Unable to feel anything in a part of the body.
examples: My fingers were {numb} with cold.
wrong: After the injection, her mouth was numb, so she could feel everything.

words.meaning: Getting better after an illness or injury.
examples: She had a bad cold, but she’s {on the mend} now.
wrong: He’s on the mend, so he’s getting sicker every day.

words.meaning: A physical or mental condition that makes some activities difficult.
examples: The building has ramps for people with a {disability}.
wrong: His disability makes everything in his daily life easier than before.

words.meaning: A person who looks after someone who is ill, old or disabled.
examples: Her {caregiver} helps her get dressed every morning.
wrong: A caregiver is someone who never looks after anyone.
